title: C282 — Air inlet door actuator
introduction:
I use this reference to connect the air inlet door actuator’s identity with its cavity drawing, circuit functions and pigtail listing. The recirculation motor and position-sensor entries tell different parts of the story: moving the door and reporting its position are separate jobs. Think of the connector table as an address book—each cavity has a location, but its Function entry tells you who lives there.

Start with CNumber and Description, find the printed cavity label in the drawing, then follow that cavity’s table row across. Finish at the pigtail listing if you need its service identifiers. This page teaches reference reading; physical access, terminal-side versus wire-side orientation, gauge convention, Size/Used code definitions, testing and replacement methods are outside its scope.

edits.why: I use the upper housing feature and the housing outline as landmarks within the printed drawing, then match its cavity labels to the table. The grey cavity corresponds to the row without a circuit or function assignment. These landmarks explain the illustration’s layout; they do not establish which side of a physical connector to view.

Read across a single cavity row to keep its circuit identifier, color code, gauge, function and terminal identifier together. The functions distinguish the recirculation-position sensor, voltage reference and reference return, and door-motor circuits. The motor descriptions retain their '(IF PLUS)' condition; those conditional direction labels are not instructions to energize a terminal or evidence that the actuator works.

I keep the Service Part identifier distinct from the Engineering Shell identifier so the service listing and housing identity do not get muddled. Gauge in this table describes the listed pigtail, while the earlier Gauge column belongs to individual circuit rows. The listing identifies a service option; it does not establish a wire-substitution, terminal-release or splice method.
